I've been farming these 8 mu for 40 years, and I've learned that steady hands make steady money. Last year my wheat averaged 540 jin per mu and maize hit 630 jin, which was decent but I think I can squeeze a bit more out if I manage the water better. My soil is loamy, and the well irrigation is reliable, but I've noticed over the years that our land here in Quzhou tends to fix phosphorus because of the high pH, so I need to put down enough P to make sure the roots can actually take it up.

For the winter wheat on all 8 mu, I'll sow an improved variety — I've been using Jimai 22 for five years now and it stands up well to the cold and doesn't lodge easily. I'll rotary till the field in early October to break up the stubble from the maize and get a fine seedbed. For fertilizer, I always calculate carefully: last year I used 15 kg of nitrogen per mu and felt the flag leaves yellowed too early, so this year I'll push it to 16 kg nitrogen per mu. I'll put down a base of 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu — that's the 15-15-15 grade — which gives me about 7.5 kg of P and 7.5 kg of K. Then I'll topdress twice with urea: 10 kg per mu at green-up, and another 10 kg per mu at jointing stage. Wait, that's too much N. Let me think again — 50 kg of 15-15-15 gives 7.5 kg N, and 20 kg of urea at 46% gives 9.2 kg N, total about 16.7 kg N. Close enough, I'll call it 16 kg N, 7 kg P, and 5 kg K per mu after adjusting the compound fertilizer slightly and accounting for what I know the soil already holds. I'll irrigate three times: once before winter to protect the seedlings from freezing, once at jointing when the stems elongate, and once at grain filling to plump the kernels. For chemicals, I'll spray a herbicide in early spring to kill the broadleaf weeds, then a fungicide at heading to prevent powdery mildew, and one insecticide if the aphids show up — so three applications total. My yield target is 550 kg per mu for wheat.

For summer maize, I'll plant Zhengdan 958 hybrid seed right after the wheat harvest in mid-June — no tillage, direct seeding into the wheat stubble. That saves me time and fuel, and the straw mulch keeps some moisture in. Maize is a hungry crop. I'll give it 16 kg nitrogen per mu too, but the timing matters more — base dressing of 40 kg compound fertilizer at sowing, then two side-dressings of urea at the big trumpet stage and tasseling. For phosphorus I'll use 5 kg per mu and potassium 5 kg per mu, which I've found keeps the stalks strong and the ears filled. I'll irrigate twice: once at the big trumpet stage and once at tasseling/silking, because that's when water stress kills your yield dead. Two pesticide sprays: a pre-emergence herbicide and one insecticide for corn borer around the heart-leaf stage. I expect 650 kg per mu from the maize if the weather cooperates.

I worry about costs every year. The fertilizer bill keeps climbing — urea went up again — but I can't afford to lose yield. A bad harvest means I eat into my savings. My neighbor Lao Wang uses about the same rates on his 10 mu, and he's had good results, so that gives me confidence I'm not throwing money away. I hire two helpers for the wheat harvest and maize sowing window because at my age I can't work that fast anymore, and that comes out of the same pocket. Still, this plan is what I know works.
